title: Target Wake Time & Battery Life
summary: Scheduled wake-ups that let badges and sensors sleep, plus protected time slots for urgent traffic.

opener.promise: Devices sleep between agreed wake-ups, so batteries can last longer
opener.problem: Badges and tags drain their batteries listening for messages that rarely come.

beats.heading: Always listening, dead by mid-shift

caption.headline: Always listening, dead by mid-shift
caption.takeaway: Radios that never sleep drain batteries, leaving clinicians or equipment unreachable until recharged.

beats.body:
[[voice-badge|Voice badges]], [[rtls|location tags]] and wearable [[patient-monitor|patient monitors]] are small, battery-powered devices. Without a schedule, their radios stay ready to listen in case the [[access-point|access point]] has something for them, and listening costs power even when nothing arrives.

The result is batteries swapped or recharged mid-shift, and devices that go quiet when a battery runs out.
beats.bottomLine: Battery swaps cost staff time and can leave clinicians or equipment unreachable until a device is recharged.
beats.sceneDescription: One hospital unit over one shift. A voice badge, a location tag and a patient monitor stand under the access point, each with a large battery above it and its radio glowing to show it is always listening. As the shift bar along the front fills, every battery drains from green through amber to red, and the badge goes dead before the shift ends. Battery levels are labeled illustrative.

callout.title: Why batteries run out
points: Radios stay awake listening, even when nothing arrives
Listening drains the battery all shift long
A dead badge or tag means an unreachable clinician or lost equipment

beats.heading: Agree when to wake, sleep in between

caption.headline: Agree when to wake, sleep in between
caption.takeaway: With [[twt|Target Wake Time]], devices sleep between agreed wake-ups{{twt-what}}, so batteries can last longer.

beats.body:
With [[twt|Target Wake Time]], each device and its access point agree when the device will wake up to exchange data, so it can sleep in between {{twt-what}}. A device can agree its own schedule, or join one the access point shares with a group of devices {{twt-types-ax}}.

TWT arrived with Wi-Fi 6 {{twt-wifi6}}. Wi-Fi 6E is Wi-Fi 6 in the 6 GHz band {{wifi6e-cert-launch}}, so it brought new spectrum, not new TWT features.
beats.bottomLine: Battery-powered clinical devices spend more time asleep, so they can last longer between charges.
beats.sceneDescription: The same shift again, now with Target Wake Time. Marks on the shift bar show the agreed wake-ups. Each device stays dark and asleep, glowing and linking to the access point only briefly at its own wake-up times. The batteries drain more slowly and have more charge left at the end of the shift. Battery levels are illustrative.

questions.q: How much longer will batteries last?
questions.a: It depends on the device and how often it must wake, so no single figure applies. Ask vendors for battery data with TWT enabled, and test with your own traffic.

questions.q: Isn’t TWT already part of Wi-Fi 6?
questions.a: Yes. TWT came with Wi-Fi 6{{twt-wifi6}}, and Wi-Fi 6E kept it as it was. Wi-Fi 7 adds Restricted TWT, which protects time slots for urgent traffic{{rtwt-be}}.

callout.title: What Target Wake Time changes
points: Each device and the access point agree when it will wake{{twt-what}}
Between wake-ups the radio sleeps and saves battery
One schedule can cover a whole group of tags{{twt-types-ax}}

cisco.text: On Cisco wireless controllers, Target Wake Time is off by default and has to be turned on{{cisco-twt-default-off}}.

beats.heading: Protected time for urgent traffic

caption.headline: Protected time for urgent traffic
caption.takeaway: Optional [[restricted-twt|Restricted TWT]] gives voice and alarms better-protected slots{{rtwt-be}}{{rtwt-optional}}.

beats.body:
TWT saves power, but it does not stop a busy laptop from using the air just when a voice packet is due. Wi-Fi 7 adds [[restricted-twt|Restricted TWT]], which reserves protected time slots for urgent traffic {{rtwt-be}}. Devices that support it finish transmitting before a protected slot begins {{rtwt-protect}}.

It is optional: only access points and devices that support it take part {{rtwt-optional}}. Where they do, voice and [[telemetry|telemetry]] can get more predictable time on the air, so include TWT and Restricted TWT in device evaluations.
beats.bottomLine: Ask device vendors about TWT and Restricted TWT: the access points enable them, but the gains appear only on devices that use them.
beats.sceneDescription: A laptop that supports Restricted TWT joins the unit, downloading over a thick link to the access point. Whenever the badge’s protected slot comes round, the laptop is marked paused, its link goes quiet, and the badge’s call goes through before the laptop resumes. A note shows that the earlier generation had no protected time slots. The badge still sleeps between wake-ups.

questions.q: Will Restricted TWT slow down other users?
questions.a: Slightly, during the protected slots: supporting devices pause before each one{{rtwt-protect}}. The slots are reserved only for traffic that needs them, such as voice and telemetry.

questions.q: Is Restricted TWT widely supported today?
questions.a: Do not assume it. It is optional in 802.11be{{rtwt-optional}}, so confirm support for each access point, device model and firmware version before relying on it.

callout.title: What Wi-Fi 7 adds
points: Optional [[restricted-twt|Restricted TWT]] protects slots for urgent traffic{{rtwt-optional}}
Check support in each access point, device and firmware

lineage.lead: First defined in IEEE 802.11ah; mainstream with Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax).

sinceWifi6.wifi6: Introduces Target Wake Time: devices sleep between agreed wake-ups{{twt-wifi6}} {{twt-what}}.
sinceWifi6.wifi6e: No TWT change: Wi-Fi 6E is Wi-Fi 6 in the 6 GHz band{{wifi6e-cert-launch}}.
sinceWifi6.wifi7: Adds optional Restricted TWT, protected slots for urgent traffic{{rtwt-be}} {{rtwt-optional}}.
